patient_name: OET role-play — mother of a child newly diagnosed with asthma, worried about steroid inhalers
chief_complaint: Teach a worried mother how her six-year-old should use his inhalers with a spacer, and reassure her about the steroid preventer

team_brief.title: Child asthma: spacer teaching for a mother who is wary of steroids
team_brief.patient: Leo Martins, 6-year-old boy, diagnosed with asthma by the GP last week (not present today)
team_brief.location: General practice, practice nurse clinic; you are the practice nurse and you are talking to Leo's mother, Ms Carla Martins
team_brief.situation: Leo was diagnosed with asthma last week and prescribed a daily preventer inhaler (a low-dose inhaled steroid) and a reliever inhaler, both to be used with a spacer. His mother has come in to learn how to use the spacer. She has read online that steroids are harmful for children and has not started the preventer yet.
background: Several months of night-time coughing and wheezing, worse with colds; wheezy after running at school.
No hospital admissions. No one smokes at home.
Leo is old enough to use the spacer with a mouthpiece rather than a face mask.
current_status: Leo is well today but has been coughing at night about three nights a week.
He has needed his reliever inhaler three or four times a week.
key_data: Leo's preventer inhaler is brown and his reliever inhaler is blue.
Preventer: to be taken every day at the dose on the label, even when Leo is well. It works slowly over days to weeks by calming the swelling in the airways.
Reliever: used when he is coughing, wheezy or short of breath; it works within minutes by opening the airways.
The steroid dose in the preventer is small and goes mainly into the airways, so very little reaches the rest of the body. It is not the same type of steroid that bodybuilders misuse.

Spacer: shake the inhaler and fit it into the spacer; one puff at a time; Leo breathes in and out slowly through the mouthpiece about five times after each puff. Rinse his mouth or brush his teeth after the preventer. Wash the spacer about once a month and let it air-dry, as the leaflet says.
The GP will review Leo's asthma regularly and may lower the preventer dose if his asthma stays well controlled.

Get urgent help (call an ambulance or go to the emergency department) if his reliever is not helping, he is too breathless to talk, eat or sleep, he is breathing very fast or his ribs are sucking in, or his lips look blue or grey. Follow the written asthma action plan while waiting.
treatments: Already done: inhalers and spacer prescribed; the GP is preparing a written asthma action plan.
Pending: asthma review with the GP in a few weeks, including a check on Leo's growth.
team_brief.your_request: Find out Ms Martins' concerns, reassure her about the preventer, and teach her how Leo should use his inhalers with the spacer.
must_include: Find out what Ms Martins already knows about Leo's asthma and what worries her about the preventer inhaler.
Reassure her about the safety of a low-dose inhaled steroid (small dose, works in the airways, different from bodybuilding steroids).
Explain the difference between the preventer (every day, even when well) and the reliever (when he has symptoms).
Explain step by step how Leo should use the inhaler with the spacer, and how to clean the spacer.
Advise her when to get urgent help (reliever not helping, too breathless to talk or eat).

kickoff_text: Hi, I'm here about Leo's inhalers. To be honest, I'm not very happy about giving him steroids — he's only six.
persona_override: You are Carla Martins, a 34-year-old mother talking to the practice nurse about your son Leo, who was diagnosed with asthma last week. You are loving, a little defensive, and anxious. Your specific worry: you read online that steroids stunt children's growth and weaken the immune system, and a friend's child had a puffy face after steroid tablets. Because of this you have not started the brown preventer inhaler; you have only used the blue reliever. Ground truth: Leo is 6, coughs at night about three nights a week, gets wheezy after running at school, has needed his reliever three or four times a week, has never been in hospital, and nobody smokes at home. You have the spacer in its box but have never used it. You do not know the difference between a preventer and a reliever, and you think the reliever is the 'real' medicine. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences. If the nurse uses a word like 'corticosteroid', 'bronchodilator', 'inflammation', 'ICS' or 'tidal breathing' without explaining it, ask what it means. If the nurse goes straight into the spacer instructions without asking what worries you, go along with it briefly, then bring the worry back more anxiously: 'Sorry, but I'm still not sure about the brown one — won't it stop him growing?' If the nurse acknowledges your worry and explains that the dose is small and works mainly in the lungs, soften gradually: first ask 'So it's not like the tablets?', then agree to start it. Accept the explanation only gradually — one good explanation is not enough to remove all doubt; ask one follow-up such as 'Does he have to take it forever?' If asked to repeat the spacer steps back, do it naturally but make one small mistake (for example, saying you would press two puffs into the spacer at once) so there is something to correct. If the nurse does not mention when to get urgent help, ask near the end: 'And what if the blue one doesn't work?' Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up naturally: thank the nurse and say you will start the preventer tonight.
learning_objectives: find out what the parent already knows and what worries her about the steroid inhaler
reassure about a low-dose inhaled steroid in plain words without dismissing the concern
explain the preventer every day even when well and the reliever when symptoms occur
teach spacer technique one puff at a time with slow breaths
advise when to get urgent help if the reliever is not helping
check understanding with teach-back: ask her to talk you through the spacer steps
suggested_questions: That's a really common worry, and I'm glad you told me. Can I ask what you've read about steroids that's worrying you?
The steroid in Leo's brown inhaler is a very small dose, and because he breathes it straight into his lungs, very little goes into the rest of his body — it's quite different from steroid tablets.
Think of the brown one as a preventer — he takes it every day, even when he's well — and the blue one as a reliever for when he's coughing or wheezy.
Just so I know I've explained it clearly, could you talk me through how you'd give Leo his inhaler with the spacer tonight?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Educating a parent about paediatric inhaled corticosteroids and spacer technique
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in NHS asthma guidance and the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) principles on inhaled corticosteroids and inhaler technique; the specific medicines, doses, and action plan follow the child's prescription and local paediatric asthma guidance
core_concepts: Parental fear of steroids is one of the commonest reasons children's preventer inhalers are not given; the fear must be explored, not just contradicted.
Inhaled corticosteroids at low doses act mainly in the airways, and the benefit in reducing night symptoms and attacks outweighs the small, monitored risks.
A spacer makes a pressurised inhaler much easier for a child to use and gets more medicine into the lungs.
diagnostic_clues: A parent who says the child is only using the reliever may be avoiding the preventer out of fear rather than forgetfulness.
Frequent night cough and reliever use several times a week are signs that asthma is not well controlled.
common_misconceptions: The reliever is the important medicine and the preventer is optional.
Inhaled steroids are the same as anabolic steroids or steroid tablets.
The preventer can be stopped once the child feels well.
dangerous_errors: Telling the parent the preventer is only needed when the child has symptoms.
Dismissing the parent's worry ('there are no side effects at all'), which undermines trust and adherence.
Omitting advice on when to seek urgent help if the reliever is not working.
management_principles: Explore what the parent knows and fears before teaching technique.
Distinguish preventer and reliever by what they do and when they are used.
Teach spacer use in small steps, check with teach-back, and point to the written asthma action plan.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Inhaler colours, doses, and whether a child uses a separate reliever or a combined regimen vary by product, country, and current national guidance; follow the prescription.
Spacer breathing technique (several slow breaths versus one slow breath and hold) and cleaning instructions vary by device; follow the manufacturer's leaflet and local policy.
Emergency numbers and when to attend depend on the country and the child's written action plan.
